incidents.cause: Failure of the brake system O-rings on the left landing gear trunnion, which allowed the hydraulic fluid to drain from the left brake system, resulting in a runway excursion and impact with a fence.

The pilot’s failure to extend the landing gear, which resulted in a gear up landing and substantial damage to the fuselage.

The pilot's decision to operate the airplane with a "dead" battery contrary to guidance provided by the Pilot's Operating Handbook. The pilot did not extend the landing gear before touchdown due to his distraction during the landing approach and his not using a landing checklist.

The pilot's failure to arrest the descent rate during an aborted simulated engine-out approach, which resulted in impact with vegetation and a subsequent cartwheel.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control on a rough surface during takeoff.
The pilot’s decision to continue the approach to land in conditions where he was unable to see in front of the airplane due to sun glare, which resulted in in a collision a building.
The pilot's failure to maintain clearance from rising terrain for undetermined reasons.

The pilot's decision to takeoff from a rough airstrip in gusty wind conditions, which resulted in a loss of control.

The pilot's loss of airplane control and his subsequent exceedance of the airplane's critical angle of attack during takeoff in variable, gusting wind conditions, which resulted in an aerodynamic stall.
The tensile overload failure of the main landing gear attachment bolt, which resulted in separation of the left main landing gear and a loss of control during landing.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing and his failure to execute a go-around.
The pilot's delayed application of carburetor heat while operating in conditions conducive to carburetor icing.

A total loss of engine power due to the separation of the No. 3 connecting rod from the crankshaft.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, which resulted in a ground loop.

The Cessna pilot’s failure to tune his radio to the common traffic advisory frequency, which resulted in a lack of awareness of the other aircraft operating at the airport. Contributing to the accident was the Cessna pilot’s lack of understanding of the airport lighting system.
The pilot's failure to extend the landing gear due to distraction and his delayed go-around, which allowed the airplane to get too low and contact the runway with the landing gear retracted.
The pilot’s failure to assure there was an adequate amount of fuel onboard to complete the flight, which resulted in a loss of engine power due to fuel exhaustion.
A total loss of left engine power due to fuel starvation as a result of the failure of the engine's electric fuel pump end cap gasket, which allowed air to be drawn into the fuel system.
The pilot’s mismanagement of the fuel supply, which resulted in a loss of engine power on the left engine due to fuel starvation.
A loss of engine power during cruise flight due to fuel exhaustion. Contributing to the accident was the pilot’s inadequate preflight and fuel planning.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during landing, resulting in a ground loop and structural damage to the airframe.
The pilot's failure to maintain aircraft control during takeoff from a rough runway surface which resulted in an off-airport forced landing just beyond the runway.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll, which resulted in a ground loop.
The pilot's decision to fly at a low altitude and his subsequent failure to see and avoid the power lines.
The failure of the overtaking airplane’s pilot to maintain visual contact and separation from the airplane being overtaken.
The restricted movement of the carburetor’s forked needle valve within its seat due to the mechanic’s misadjustment of the valve clip forks, which resulted in fuel starvation.
The pilot's decision to attempt low-altitude flight and his failure to maintain adequate clearance from power lines.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during landing.
The student pilot’s failure to maintain directional control of the tailwheel-equipped airplane during the landing roll.
An encounter with instrument meteorological conditions, which resulted in the  pilot's spatial disorientation and a loss of airplane control.
The pilot's failure to maintain directional control during a takeoff attempt.
The flight instructor's failure to maintain directional control during landing, in cross wind conditions.
The pilot’s failure to maintain directional control during the landing roll.

The student pilot’s hard landing and subsequent loss of directional control.
The pilot’s improper recovery from a bounced landing, which resulted in a loss of directional control and subsequent runway excursion.
The pilot's inadvertent and excessive application of brake pressure during landing, which resulted in a nose over.
The pilot's failure to maintain control of the airplane while landing in gusting wind conditions.
